turns.doctor_question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?
turns.patient_response:
Well, honestly, my boss kind of sent me here. I mean, it was a strong suggestion, if you know what I mean. I've been doing general maintenance and repair work for a long time, and usually, you know, I can handle the physical day-to-day stuff—fixing a leaky trap, patching drywall, whatever. But lately... well, it’s just gotten really, really bad. I keep completely dropping the ball on the communication side of things. Like, I’ll get a work order, go look at it, realize I need a specific part from the supply house, and tell the tenant or the manager I’ll call them back by noon with an update. But then I just... I completely forget the scheduled callback. Or I'll set the actual work order clipboard down somewhere and just lose it entirely. 

It’s not just one or two isolated things either, it’s basic follow-ups I promised people to their faces, and it just totally slips my mind the second I walk away. And now, I mean, the unfinished tickets and the missed messages have just piled up so much. My truck is a mess of lost sticky notes. The worst part is, there's a senior supervisor position opening up, and I really, really want it—I've put in the years—but work basically pulled me aside and told me I need to get whatever this is sorted out. They actually made the appointment for me to come here because they said if I don't fix this, I'm going to completely lose my shot at moving up. Because, I mean, you can't be managing a team if you can't even remember to call a vendor back, right? So, yeah, that's why I'm sitting here. It's just incredibly frustrating because I know how to do my job, I just can't seem to keep the details in my head long enough to finish the loop, you know?

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes failing to finish duties in the workplace, noting that unfinished tickets and missed messages have piled up.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient mentions their truck is a mess of lost sticky notes and tasks have piled up, indicating difficulty organizing activities.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states they set down and lose necessary items like their work order clipboard and sticky notes.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient reports frequently forgetting daily work activities, such as scheduled callbacks and basic follow-ups they promised to do.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have this same kind of trouble with attention or forgetting things when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it’s funny you ask that because I was just thinking about this the other day when I was trying to find a work order I lost in my truck. I remember being exactly like this way back in grade school, you know? Long before I ever had a job or a boss breathing down my neck or any of this pressure to get a promotion. 

I mean, I can picture it so clearly. I was always the kid who was, like, frantically searching through my desk while everyone else was already working. My teachers, they were always telling my parents, "Oh, she's so bright, she's a smart girl," but then in the same breath, it was always, "but she just can't keep track of her things." I lost assignments all the time. I'd do the homework, I swear I would, and then it would just vanish into thin air between my house and the classroom. And directions! Oh my gosh, if a teacher gave us, like, three steps to do something, I'd hear the first one, maybe the second one, and then my brain would just kind of... float away. I'd always be the one leaning over to the kid next to me whispering, "Wait, what are we supposed to be doing right now?" 

I constantly needed reminders to just finish my classwork. Like, I’d start a worksheet, get halfway through, and then suddenly I’m staring out the window at a bird or something, completely forgetting that I was in the middle of a math problem. It was so frustrating, even back then, because I knew I wasn't stupid, you know? I just couldn't seem to make my brain hold onto the things it was supposed to hold onto. It’s like there was a leak in my memory or my attention span, and all the important stuff just kept draining out. So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing, it’s just... it’s just causing a lot more trouble for me now as an adult with actual responsibilities.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes being unable to sustain attention on classwork, getting halfway through a worksheet before losing focus.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient notes that when spoken to with directions, she would only hear the first part before her brain would 'float away'.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly states she could not follow through on multi-step directions and constantly needed reminders to finish her classwork.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports frequently losing assignments and having to frantically search her desk for misplaced items.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as staring out the window at a bird while in the middle of a math problem.

turns.doctor_question: As a child, were you often fidgety or unable to stay seated when you were expected to?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, I wasn't one of those kids bouncing off the walls, you know? It's funny you bring that up because my brother, now he was a handful. He couldn't sit still if his life depended on it. My mom used to say he had ants in his pants. He was always tapping his foot, drumming his fingers on the table, getting up to sharpen his pencil five times during a spelling test. The teachers were constantly telling him to sit down and stop disrupting the class. But me? No, I was perfectly fine just sitting there. 

I'd be at my desk, quiet as a mouse, not bothering anybody. That was the thing, I wasn't causing a scene. I was just... somewhere else in my head. Like I said, I'd be staring out the window, looking at the clouds, or maybe just staring at a smudge on my desk, totally lost in thought about whatever movie I watched the night before or what I was going to have for lunch. I could sit in that hard little wooden chair for the whole period without moving a muscle, honestly. It was almost like I was too still, you know? Because my body was there, parked right in seat number four, third row back, but my brain was on a completely different planet. 

So the teachers didn't really yell at me for getting out of my seat or fidgeting around. They'd just suddenly call my name, and I'd jump because I hadn't heard a single word they said for the last ten minutes. I didn't need to run around the room; I just needed someone to snap their fingers in front of my face to bring me back down to earth. I was the daydreamer, not the troublemaker. It's actually kind of why I think I flew under the radar for so long, because if you're not loud and you're not running around the classroom, people just assume you're paying attention, right? But yeah, no, I didn't have that physical restless thing going on at all. Just the... the mental drifting, I guess you'd call it.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes not hearing a single word the teacher said and jumping when their name was called, indicating difficulty listening.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being a 'daydreamer' who was 'totally lost in thought' and experiencing 'mental drifting' while staring out the window.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies fidgeting, stating they could sit without moving a muscle and did not have any physical restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient denies getting out of their seat, noting they were perfectly fine just sitting there and teachers didn't yell at them for leaving their seat.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient denies running around or being physically restless, stating they were not 'bouncing off the walls'.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of work, do these attention and forgetting problems also cause trouble in your day-to-day life?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I mean... at home, sure, my apartment is a bit of a mess, and I might leave the laundry in the washer for three days until it smells and I have to run it again. But honestly, I can't even really think about my personal life right now because my mind is just completely consumed by what's happening at the property. I know you're asking about outside of work, but the work thing has just turned into such a serious, serious issue that it's literally all I can focus on. 

Like I mentioned earlier about them sending me here... it's not just a friendly suggestion anymore. It's a full-blown crisis. I have this massive backlog of unfinished tickets that is just haunting me. Half of them are on my clipboard, half are floating around the cab of my truck, and I don't even know where to start. And because I keep dropping the ball on the follow-ups, the tenant complaints are just piling up at the management office. Just last week, a tenant in building four called corporate on me because I told her I was going to grab a replacement aerator for her faucet and I completely forgot and never went back. She waited around all day. 

But the thing that really keeps me up at night, the thing that is just making my stomach tie itself into knots, is that I actually have a safety review on my record now. Yeah. I was working in one of the utility rooms, got distracted trying to remember if I had ordered a specific size of copper piping, walked away to check my phone, and just completely forgot I left the electrical panel wide open. The property manager walked through and found it. So now there's an official safety ding in my file. 

After all my years of hard work, I am just so incredibly scared that all of this is going to completely cost me the promotion path I’ve been working toward. I've put my blood, sweat, and tears into this place, and now they're looking at a backlog, angry

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient fails to finish workplace duties, evidenced by a massive backlog of unfinished tickets and failing to return to complete a tenant's faucet repair.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient demonstrates difficulty organizing tasks, noting that work tickets are scattered between a clipboard and their truck and they don't know where to start.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being distracted from a task by unrelated thoughts about ordering piping and checking their phone.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient is forgetful in daily activities, such as forgetting laundry in the washer for days and forgetting to return to a tenant's apartment.

turns.doctor_question: When you're not thinking about work, do you still find yourself feeling anxious or on edge much of the time?
turns.patient_response:
No, honestly... not really. I mean, if I can actually get my brain to shut off about the property and the tickets and the safety review—which, I'll admit, is pretty hard to do right now—but if I *do* manage to just be at home and not dwell on it, no, I'm not an anxious person at all. I don't have that... that constant on-edge feeling you're talking about, not naturally. 

Like, if you take work out of the equation entirely, I'm actually a really laid-back person. Almost to a fault, probably. My ex used to complain all the time that nothing bothered me enough. Like, if the sink was backed up at our place, I’d just shrug and say I’d snake the drain when I got around to it, and I wouldn't lose a single wink of sleep over it. I can just sit out on my patio on a Sunday morning with a cup of coffee, listening to the radio, maybe tinkering with a busted toaster or whatever, and I am perfectly calm. My heart's not racing, my stomach isn't in knots, I'm not worrying about the future or... or the state of the world or whatever else people get anxious about. I'm just there. I can just chill. 

So, no, I don't have this general anxiety thing going on in the background of my life. It really is just... it's just this job situation. Because like I was saying before, I've put years of sweat into this company, and the thought of losing my promotion path just because my brain decided to check out and leave an electrical panel open... it's a very specific, very real threat to my livelihood, you know? It's a rational thing to be stressed about. But if you take that crisis away, I'm honestly fine. Just a regular, easygoing person who happens to leave her coffee mug in the microwave for two days. I don't walk around feeling nervous for no reason.
